## 5.6 Fault Classification Standards Refinement

### 5.6.1 P1-Level Fault (Urgent Fault) Detailed Definition

**Business Impact Definition:**
A P1-level fault is a fault that causes the complete unavailability of core business systems, resulting in total interruption of the Government Service Hall's main business functions. Core business systems include but are not limited to: Government Service Comprehensive Acceptance System, Unified Identity Authentication System, Electronic Certificate System, Data Sharing and Exchange Platform, etc. When any of the above systems is completely unavailable without an effective alternative, it is classified as a P1-level fault.

**User Impact Definition:**
P1-level faults affect all users of Government Service Hall services, including:
- Citizens and businesses conducting on-site transactions (daily impact ≥500 person-times);
- Users conducting online transactions (daily impact ≥2,000 person-times);
- All Government Service Hall staff (≥200 persons);
- Related government department data exchange operations.

**Data Impact Definition:**
P1-level faults may cause the following data risks:
- Business data loss or corruption risk;
- Data synchronization interruption, leading to data inconsistency;
- Data backup interruption, leading to incomplete backup data;
- Sensitive data leakage risk.

**Response Time Requirements:**
- Hotline response time: Immediate answer (≤5 seconds);
- Work order dispatch time: ≤3 minutes;
- Engineer confirmation time: ≤5 minutes;
- On-site arrival time: ≤15 minutes;
- Initial handling commencement time: ≤10 minutes;
- Business recovery time: ≤1 hour (target), ≤2 hours (maximum).

**Escalation Rules:**
- If fault cause is not confirmed within 10 minutes of fault occurrence, automatically escalate to O&M project manager;
- If business recovery has not commenced within 30 minutes of fault occurrence, automatically escalate to company senior management;
- If business has not recovered within 1 hour of fault occurrence, initiate company-level emergency response;
- If business has not recovered within 2 hours of fault occurrence, initiate cross-company joint emergency mechanism.

**Handling Time Limits:**
- Fault confirmation: ≤10 minutes;
- Fault localization: ≤20 minutes;
- Temporary recovery plan implementation: ≤30 minutes;
- Permanent fix plan implementation: ≤1 hour;
- Full business recovery verification: ≤1 hour;
- Fault report submission: ≤2 hours.

### 5.6.2 P2-Level Fault (Important Fault) Detailed Definition

**Business Impact Definition:**
A P2-level fault is a fault that causes severe performance degradation or partial unavailability of important business systems, resulting in more than 50% of Government Service Hall business functions being significantly affected. Important business systems include but are not limited to: Queue Management System, Electronic Supervision System, Performance Assessment System, Financial Management System, Office Automation System, etc. When the above systems experience performance degradation exceeding 50% or partial function unavailability, it is classified as a P2-level fault.

**User Impact Definition:**
P2-level fault impact scope includes:
- Citizens and businesses conducting on-site transactions (daily impact 200-500 person-times);
- Some users conducting online transactions (daily impact 500-2,000 person-times);
- Some Government Service Hall staff (50-200 persons);
- Some government department data exchange operations.

**Data Impact Definition:**
P2-level faults may cause the following data risks:
- Business data processing delays or backlogs;
- Partial data synchronization abnormalities;
- Data backup delays;
- Data integrity threatened.

**Response Time Requirements:**
- Hotline response time: ≤10 seconds;
- Work order dispatch time: ≤5 minutes;
- Engineer confirmation time: ≤5 minutes;
- On-site arrival time: ≤30 minutes;
- Initial handling commencement time: ≤15 minutes;
- Business recovery time: ≤2 hours (target), ≤4 hours (maximum).

**Escalation Rules:**
- If fault cause is not confirmed within 20 minutes of fault occurrence, automatically escalate to O&M project manager;
- If business recovery has not commenced within 1 hour of fault occurrence, automatically escalate to company senior management;
- If business has not recovered within 2 hours of fault occurrence, initiate company-level emergency response.

**Handling Time Limits:**
- Fault confirmation: ≤15 minutes;
- Fault localization: ≤30 minutes;
- Temporary recovery plan implementation: ≤1 hour;
- Permanent fix plan implementation: ≤2 hours;
- Full business recovery verification: ≤2 hours;
- Fault report submission: ≤4 hours.

### 5.6.3 P3-Level Fault (General Fault) Detailed Definition

**Business Impact Definition:**
A P3-level fault is a fault that causes non-core system failures, having certain but controllable impact on Government Service Hall operations. Non-core systems include but are not limited to: Information Display System, Meeting Room Reservation System, Attendance Management System, Asset Management System, etc. When the above systems experience faults but do not affect main business processing, it is classified as a P3-level fault.

**User Impact Definition:**
P3-level fault impact scope includes:
- Some users conducting on-site transactions (daily impact <200 person-times);
- A small number of Government Service Hall staff (<50 persons);
- Business can continue through alternative methods.

**Data Impact Definition:**
P3-level faults may cause the following data risks:
- Non-core business data processing delays;
- Some statistical data inaccuracies;
- No direct impact on core business data.

**Response Time Requirements:**
- Hotline response time: ≤15 seconds;
- Work order dispatch time: ≤10 minutes;
- Engineer confirmation time: ≤10 minutes;
- On-site arrival time: ≤60 minutes;
- Initial handling commencement time: ≤30 minutes;
- Business recovery time: ≤4 hours (target), ≤8 hours (maximum).

**Escalation Rules:**
- If fault cause is not confirmed within 30 minutes of fault occurrence, automatically escalate to on-duty supervisor;
- If business has not recovered within 2 hours of fault occurrence, automatically escalate to O&M project manager.

**Handling Time Limits:**
- Fault confirmation: ≤30 minutes;
- Fault localization: ≤1 hour;
- Temporary recovery plan implementation: ≤2 hours;
- Permanent fix plan implementation: ≤4 hours;
- Full business recovery verification: ≤4 hours;
- Fault report submission: ≤8 hours.

### 5.6.4 P4-Level Fault (Minor Fault) Detailed Definition

**Business Impact Definition:**
A P4-level fault is a minor fault or optimization need that does not affect business operations. These include but are not limited to: equipment indicator abnormalities that do not affect functionality, system log alerts with no actual impact, performance optimization needs, interface display abnormalities that do not affect operations, etc.

**User Impact Definition:**
P4-level faults have virtually no impact on users and do not affect the normal processing of any business.

**Data Impact Definition:**
P4-level faults have no impact on data.

**Response Time Requirements:**
- Hotline response time: ≤20 seconds;
- Work order dispatch time: ≤15 minutes;
- Engineer confirmation time: ≤15 minutes;
- On-site arrival time: ≤120 minutes;
- Initial handling commencement time: ≤60 minutes;
- Business recovery time: ≤8 hours (target), ≤24 hours (maximum).

**Escalation Rules:**
- If not recovered within 4 hours of fault occurrence, automatically escalate to on-duty supervisor;
- If not completely resolved within 7 days after handling, escalate to O&M project manager.

**Handling Time Limits:**
- Fault confirmation: ≤60 minutes;
- Fault localization: ≤2 hours;
- Fix plan implementation: ≤8 hours;
- Business recovery verification: ≤8 hours;
- Fault report submission: ≤24 hours.

## 5.7 Fault Escalation Mechanism

### 5.7.1 Escalation Matrix

Fault handling establishes a five-level escalation matrix to ensure faults receive resource investment and management attention commensurate with their severity:

**Level 1: On-Duty Engineer Level (L1)**
- Applicable Faults: Initial handling stage of P3 and P4 level faults;
- Handling Personnel: On-duty engineer;
- Authority Scope: Can execute standard handling plans, use routine tools and spare parts;
- Escalation Conditions: Handling time exceeds 30 minutes without resolution, or problems encountered beyond capability scope.

**Level 2: On-Duty Supervisor Level (L2)**
- Applicable Faults: Initial handling of P2 level faults, or P3/P4 level faults after L1 escalation;
- Handling Personnel: On-duty supervisor;
- Authority Scope: Can mobilize more resources, coordinate multiple engineers for collaborative handling;
- Escalation Conditions: Handling time exceeds 1 hour without resolution, or faults involving multi-system coordinated failures.

**Level 3: O&M Project Manager Level (L3)**
- Applicable Faults: Initial handling of P1 level faults, or P2 level faults after L2 escalation;
- Handling Personnel: O&M project manager;
- Authority Scope: Can mobilize all O&M resources, coordinate external vendor support, initiate emergency plans;
- Escalation Conditions: Handling time exceeds 2 hours without resolution, or faults involving major data security incidents.

**Level 4: Company Senior Management Level (L4)**
- Applicable Faults: P1 level faults after L3 escalation, or major data security incidents;
- Handling Personnel: Company deputy general manager or general manager;
- Authority Scope: Can mobilize all company resources, initiate cross-company joint emergency response, coordinate with government authorities;
- Escalation Conditions: Business has not recovered after 4 hours, or faults involving significant social impact.

**Level 5: Joint Emergency Level (L5)**
- Applicable Faults: Extraordinarily major faults requiring multi-party joint handling;
- Handling Personnel: Joint Emergency Command (including O&M team, equipment vendors, operators, government authorities, etc.);
- Authority Scope: Can mobilize all relevant party resources, initiate highest-level emergency response;
- Escalation Conditions: Extraordinarily major faults that cannot be independently handled at the company level.

### 5.7.2 Notification Rules

**L1 Level Notification:**
- Notification Recipients: On-duty engineer personally;
- Notification Method: System automatic dispatch;
- Notification Content: Work order details, fault description, handling suggestions.

**L2 Level Notification:**
- Notification Recipients: On-duty supervisor, on-duty engineer;
- Notification Method: System notification + SMS;
- Notification Content: Escalation reason, current handling status, suggested escalation plan.

**L3 Level Notification:**
- Notification Recipients: O&M project manager, on-duty supervisor, on-duty engineer, Procuring Entity O&M responsible person;
- Notification Method: System notification + SMS + telephone;
- Notification Content: Fault details, impact scope, measures taken, resources requiring coordination.

**L4 Level Notification:**
- Notification Recipients: Company senior management, O&M project manager, Procuring Entity supervising leader, Procuring Entity senior leadership;
- Notification Method: System notification + SMS + telephone + email;
- Notification Content: Fault details, impact scope, measures taken, estimated recovery time, matters requiring company-level coordination.

**L5 Level Notification:**
- Notification Recipients: All Joint Emergency Command members, government authorities, relevant vendors;
- Notification Method: Telephone + email + formal letter;
- Notification Content: Fault details, impact scope, responsibilities of each party, joint handling plan.

### 5.7.3 Escalation Time Limits

**Automatic Escalation Time Limits:**
- P1-level fault: Automatically escalate one level if not recovered within 30 minutes;
- P2-level fault: Automatically escalate one level if not recovered within 1 hour;
- P3-level fault: Automatically escalate one level if not recovered within 2 hours;
- P4-level fault: Automatically escalate one level if not recovered within 4 hours.

**Manual Escalation Time Limits:**
- When on-duty engineer determines escalation is needed, must complete escalation request within 5 minutes;
- On-duty supervisor must complete escalation request approval within 3 minutes;
- O&M project manager must complete escalation request handling within 5 minutes;
- Company senior management must complete escalation request handling within 10 minutes.

**Escalation Response Time Limits:**
- L1→L2 escalation: On-duty supervisor must respond within 10 minutes;
- L2→L3 escalation: O&M project manager must respond within 15 minutes;
- L3→L4 escalation: Company senior management must respond within 30 minutes;
- L4→L5 escalation: Joint Emergency Command must respond within 1 hour.

## 5.8 Fault Root Cause Analysis Methods

### 5.8.1 5-Why Analysis Method Template

**Method Overview:**
The 5-Why Analysis method is an analytical approach that explores the root cause of a problem through successive questioning of "why." Proposed by Toyota, it is one of the core tools of lean management and problem analysis. Through layer-by-layer analysis, it avoids remaining at surface phenomena, finding the root cause and developing effective corrective measures.

**Detailed Steps:**

**Step 1: Define the Problem**
- Clearly and accurately describe the problem symptoms;
- Quantify the problem's impact (time, scope, degree);
- Determine the problem's occurrence time and discovery time;
- Record the discovery method and discoverer.

**Example:**
Problem: The Government Service Comprehensive Acceptance System experienced downtime on June 8, 2026, at 10:00, causing complete interruption of all hall operations, affecting approximately 500 citizens.

**Step 2: First Question — Why?**
- Ask "why" directly regarding the problem symptoms;
- Answer based on facts and data, without making assumptions;
- Record the answer.

**Example:**
Q: Why did the Government Service Comprehensive Acceptance System experience downtime?
A: Because the database server CPU usage reached 100%, making the system unresponsive.

**Step 3: Second Question — Why?**
- Continue asking "why" based on the first answer;
- Continue answering based on facts and data;
- Record the answer.

**Example:**
Q: Why did the database server CPU usage reach 100%?
A: Because a query statement was performing large numbers of full table scans, consuming substantial CPU resources.

**Step 4: Third Question — Why?**
- Continue asking "why" based on the second answer;
- Continue answering based on facts and data;
- Record the answer.

**Example:**
Q: Why was the query statement performing large numbers of full table scans?
A: Because the query statement lacked effective indexes, causing the database engine to choose full table scans.

**Step 5: Fourth Question — Why?**
- Continue asking "why" based on the third answer;
- Continue answering based on facts and data;
- Record the answer.

**Example:**
Q: Why did the query statement lack effective indexes?
A: Because a new query function was recently added, and the developer did not perform index optimization on the SQL statement for that function.

**Step 6: Fifth Question — Why?**
- Continue asking "why" based on the fourth answer;
- Find the root cause;
- Record the answer.

**Example:**
Q: Why did the developer not perform index optimization on the SQL statement for that function?
A: Because there is no SQL performance review process, and SQL performance evaluation was not conducted before the new function went live.

**Step 7: Develop Corrective Measures**
- Develop corrective measures based on the root cause;
- Develop preventive measures to prevent similar problems from recurring;
- Specify responsible persons and completion deadlines.

**Example:**
Corrective Measures:
1. Immediately add indexes to SQL statements lacking indexes (Responsible Person: Database Administrator, Completion Deadline: 1 hour);
2. Establish SQL performance review process, requiring SQL performance evaluation before all new functions go live (Responsible Person: Technical Manager, Completion Deadline: 1 week);
3. Conduct performance review of all existing SQL statements to identify potential performance issues (Responsible Person: Development Team, Completion Deadline: 1 month).

### 5.8.2 Fishbone Diagram Analysis Method Template

**Method Overview:**
The Fishbone Diagram (also known as Cause-and-Effect Diagram or Ishikawa Diagram) is a visualization tool for analyzing potential causes of a problem. Proposed by Japanese quality management expert Kaoru Ishikawa, it places the problem at the "fish head" position and distributes possible causes by category along the "fish bones," helping teams comprehensively and systematically analyze potential causes of problems.

**Fishbone Diagram Classification Dimensions (6M):**
- **Man**: Personnel skills, operational errors, insufficient communication, etc.;
- **Machine**: Equipment faults, hardware aging, configuration errors, etc.;
- **Material**: Data quality, documentation completeness, spare parts quality, etc.;
- **Method**: Process deficiencies, insufficient operating standards, system gaps, etc.;
- **Environment**: Data center environment, network environment, temperature and humidity, etc.;
- **Measurement**: Insufficient monitoring, alarm delays, measurement errors, etc.

**Detailed Steps:**

**Step 1: Identify the Problem**
- Write the problem on the right side of the fishbone diagram (fish head position);
- Ensure the problem description is clear, specific, and quantifiable.

**Step 2: Determine Main Classification Dimensions**
- Select appropriate classification dimensions based on the nature of the problem;
- The 6M classification dimensions are typically used, and can be adjusted based on actual conditions.

**Step 3: Brainstorm Causes**
- Organize relevant personnel (O&M engineers, developers, management, etc.) for brainstorming;
- List all possible causes for each classification dimension;
- Encourage free expression without criticizing any ideas.

**Step 4: Draw the Fishbone Diagram**
- Organize collected causes by classification dimension;
- Draw the fishbone diagram, labeling causes on corresponding fishbone branches;
- Use different colors to mark high-probability causes.

**Step 5: Analyze and Determine Root Causes**
- Analyze and screen all causes on the fishbone diagram;
- Confirm root causes through data verification, experimental testing, etc.;
- Root causes typically concentrate on 2-3 main causes.

**Step 6: Develop Improvement Measures**
- Develop specific improvement measures based on root causes;
- Specify responsible persons and completion deadlines;
- Develop effect verification methods.

**Example: Fishbone Diagram Analysis for "Database Query Performance Degradation"**

Fish Head: Database Query Performance Degradation

Man:
- Developers lack SQL writing experience
- Insufficient database performance optimization training
- O&M personnel failed to detect performance anomalies promptly

Machine:
- Insufficient database server CPU resources
- Insufficient memory configuration
- Disk I/O performance bottleneck

Material:
- Rapid data volume growth
- Poor data quality leading to low query efficiency
- Lack of data archiving strategy

Method:
- Lack of SQL performance review process
- Unreasonable index design
- Missing query optimization process

Environment:
- Surge in concurrent users
- Increased network latency
- Excessive data center temperature

Measurement:
- Lack of database performance monitoring
- Unreasonable alarm threshold settings
- Performance baseline not established

### 5.8.3 FTA (Fault Tree Analysis) Method Template

**Method Overview:**
FTA (Fault Tree Analysis) is a top-down deductive analysis method that uses logic gates (AND gates, OR gates) to link top-level events (faults) with bottom-level events (root causes), helping analysts comprehensively understand fault occurrence paths and probabilities. This method is widely used in high-reliability fields such as aerospace, nuclear energy, and rail transit.

**Detailed Steps:**

**Step 1: Define the Top-Level Event**
- Clearly define the fault event to be analyzed (top-level event);
- Ensure the top-level event definition is clear and quantifiable.

**Step 2: Identify Intermediate Events**
- Identify direct causes leading to the top-level event (intermediate events);
- Intermediate events are logical nodes between the top-level event and basic events.

**Step 3: Identify Basic Events**
- Identify basic causes leading to intermediate events (basic events);
- Basic events are the indivisible bottom-level causes.

**Step 4: Establish Logical Relationships**
- Use logic gates (AND gates, OR gates) to establish logical relationships between events;
- AND gate: Output event occurs only when all input events occur simultaneously;
- OR gate: Output event occurs when any input event occurs.

**Step 5: Calculate Fault Probability**
- Calculate the probability of the top-level event based on the occurrence probability of basic events;
- Identify minimal cut sets (the minimum basic event combinations leading to the top-level event);
- Evaluate the importance of each basic event.

**Step 6: Develop Improvement Measures**
- Develop improvement measures for high-importance basic events;
- Reduce the occurrence probability of critical basic events;
- Add redundancy design to reduce system fault risk.

**Example: FTA Analysis for "Core Business System Downtime"**

Top-Level Event: Core Business System Downtime

Intermediate Events (OR gate):
- Database server failure
- Application server failure
- Network connection interruption
- Power supply system failure

Database Server Failure (OR gate):
- Hardware failure (disk damage, memory failure)
- Software failure (database process crash)
- Performance failure (CPU/memory resources exhausted)
- Human operational error (accidental data deletion, accidental configuration change)

Application Server Failure (OR gate):
- Application process crash
- Memory leak
- Configuration error
- Patch compatibility issue

Network Connection Interruption (OR gate):
- Core switch failure
- Fiber optic link interruption
- Operator line failure
- Network attack

Power Supply System Failure (OR gate):
- Mains power interruption
- UPS failure
- Power distribution cabinet failure
- Backup generator failure

## 5.9 Fault Knowledge Base Construction Plan

### 5.9.1 Knowledge Base Classification System

The fault knowledge base adopts a four-level classification system to ensure knowledge entries are structurally clear and easily searchable:

**Level 1 Classification (By System Type):**
- Hardware System Knowledge Base
- Software System Knowledge Base
- Network System Knowledge Base
- Security System Knowledge Base
- Infrastructure Knowledge Base

**Level 2 Classification (By Equipment/System Brand or Model):**
- Hardware Systems: Servers, Storage Devices, Terminal Equipment, Security Equipment, etc.
- Software Systems: Operating Systems, Databases, Middleware, Application Software, etc.
- Network Systems: Switches, Routers, Firewalls, Load Balancers, etc.
- Infrastructure: UPS, Air Conditioning, Fire Suppression, Structured Cabling, etc.

**Level 3 Classification (By Fault Type):**
- Performance Fault Category
- Functional Fault Category
- Connection Fault Category
- Security Fault Category
- Configuration Fault Category

**Level 4 Classification (By Fault Symptom):**
- Specific fault symptoms and corresponding solutions

### 5.9.2 Knowledge Entry Entry Standards

**Knowledge Entry Standard Format:**

| Field Name | Field Description | Required |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Knowledge ID | System auto-generated, format: KB-YYYYMMDD-XXXX | Yes |
| Fault Title | Brief and concise fault symptom description | Yes |
| System Classification | Level 1/Level 2/Level 3/Level 4 classification | Yes |
| Fault Symptoms | Detailed fault manifestation description, including screenshots/logs | Yes |
| Fault Cause | Root cause analysis results | Yes |
| Impact Scope | Affected systems, users, business | Yes |
| Solution | Detailed resolution steps and operational guide | Yes |
| Preventive Measures | Measures to prevent similar faults from recurring | No |
| Required Tools | Tools and spare parts needed for handling the fault | No |
| Handling Duration | Estimated handling time | Yes |
| Difficulty Level | Junior/Intermediate/Senior | Yes |
| Related Knowledge | Related knowledge entry IDs | No |
| Creator | Knowledge entry creator | Yes |
| Creation Time | Knowledge entry creation time | Yes |
| Reviewer | Knowledge entry reviewer | Yes |
| Review Time | Knowledge entry review time | Yes |
| Version Number | Knowledge entry version number | Yes |
| Usage Count | Number of times the knowledge entry has been referenced | Yes |

**Entry Quality Requirements:**
- Fault symptom descriptions must be clear and accurate, including specific error codes, log excerpts, screenshots, and other evidence;
- Solution steps must be detailed and actionable, including command lines, configuration parameters, operational screenshots, etc.;
- All knowledge entries must be reviewed by the technical supervisor before entering the knowledge base;
- Knowledge entries must be updated monthly to ensure content timeliness.

### 5.9.3 Knowledge Base Search Mechanism

**Search Methods:**
- **Keyword Search**: Supports search by fault symptoms, error codes, equipment models, and other keywords;
- **Classification Search**: Filters layer by layer through the four-level classification system;
- **Intelligent Search**: Based on natural language processing technology, understands user query intent and returns the most relevant knowledge entries;
- **Related Search**: Views related knowledge of the current knowledge entry, expanding the search scope.

**Search Priority Rules:**
1. Exact match takes priority over fuzzy match;
2. Knowledge entries with higher usage counts are displayed first;
3. Recently updated knowledge entries are displayed first;
4. Knowledge entries with difficulty levels matching the current user's skill level are displayed first.

### 5.9.4 Knowledge Base Update Process

**Regular Updates:**
- The knowledge base administrator conducts a comprehensive review of the knowledge base monthly;
- Delete outdated or no longer applicable knowledge entries;
- Update solutions or preventive measures of existing knowledge entries;
- Compile knowledge base usage data and identify knowledge gaps.

**Immediate Updates:**
- After each P1 and P2 level fault handling is complete, handling experience must be entered into the knowledge base within 48 hours;
- For new types of faults, new knowledge entries must be created within 24 hours after handling completion;
- For optimization solutions to existing knowledge entries, immediate updates after review approval.

**Annual Review:**
- Organize knowledge base annual review meeting every December;
- Invite O&M team, development team, and management to participate;
- Evaluate the completeness, accuracy, and practicality of the knowledge base;
- Develop the following year's knowledge base construction plan.

## 5.10 Major Fault Handling Plan

### 5.10.1 Communication Assurance Plan

**Communication Group Settings:**

| Group Name | Members | Purpose | Priority |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Emergency Command Group | O&M project manager, company senior management, Procuring Entity senior leadership | P1-level fault emergency command | Highest |
| Technical Handling Group | All O&M team members, technical experts | Technical problem discussion and handling | High |
| Vendor Coordination Group | O&M project manager, vendor liaison persons | External resource coordination | High |
| User Notification Group | Procuring Entity department heads, hall window supervisors | Fault notification and progress updates | Medium |
| O&M Daily Group | All O&M team members | Daily work communication | Normal |

**Communication Assurance Measures:**
- All emergency communication groups operate on a 7×24-hour online system;
- Emergency Command Group members must keep their phones accessible with ringtones on;
- Equipped with backup communication methods (walkie-talkies, satellite phones) to ensure communication continuity under extreme conditions;
- Test communication group availability once per quarter.

### 5.10.2 Data Recovery Plan

**Data Recovery Strategy:**

| Recovery Scenario | Recovery Method | RPO (Recovery Point Objective) | RTO (Recovery Time Objective) |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Database logical error | Recover to most recent backup point based on backup files | ≤1 hour | ≤4 hours |
| Database physical damage | Switch to backup database, repair main database | ≤5 minutes | ≤2 hours |
| File system damage | Recovery based on snapshots or backup recovery | ≤4 hours | ≤8 hours |
| Storage device failure | Switch to backup storage device, replace faulty device | ≤5 minutes | ≤4 hours |
| Ransomware attack | Isolate infected area, recover based on offline backup | ≤24 hours | ≤48 hours |

**Data Recovery Process:**
1. Assess the scope of data loss and extent of damage;
2. Determine the optimal recovery method (backup recovery, snapshot recovery, off-site recovery);
3. Execute data recovery operations;
4. Verify data integrity and consistency;
5. Restore business system access;
6. Prepare data recovery report.

### 5.10.3 Business Continuity Plan

**Business Continuity Levels:**

| Business System | Continuity Level | Recovery Time Limit | Alternative Plan |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Government Service Comprehensive Acceptance System | Highest | ≤1 hour | Manual acceptance, paper materials |
| Unified Identity Authentication System | High | ≤2 hours | Temporary identity verification plan |
| Electronic Certificate System | High | ≤2 hours | Manual certificate verification |
| Data Sharing and Exchange Platform | Medium | ≤4 hours | Manual data exchange |
| Queue Management System | Medium | ≤2 hours | Manual queue guidance |
| Electronic Supervision System | Low | ≤8 hours | Manual patrol inspection |

**Business Continuity Assurance Measures:**
- Core business systems use dual-machine hot standby to ensure single-point failures do not affect operations;
- Critical data is synchronized to the disaster recovery center in real-time to ensure data security;
- Detailed business switching plans are developed, specifying switching steps and responsible persons;
- Business continuity drills are conducted once every six months to verify plan effectiveness.

## 5.11 Fault Retrospective Mechanism

### 5.11.1 Retrospective Process Template

**Retrospective Meeting Organization:**
- **Chairperson**: O&M project manager (P1-level faults chaired by company senior management);
- **Participants**: Fault handling related personnel, technical experts, management representatives;
- **Meeting Time**: Within 48 hours after fault recovery;
- **Meeting Duration**: 1-2 hours.

**Retrospective Meeting Agenda:**

| No. | Agenda Content | Time Allocation | Responsible Person |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | Fault Overview (timeline, impact scope) | 10 minutes | On-duty supervisor |
| 2 | Handling Process Review (response, diagnosis, repair) | 15 minutes | Handling engineer |
| 3 | Highlights Summary (aspects done well) | 10 minutes | Open discussion |
| 4 | Problem Analysis (shortcomings and root causes) | 20 minutes | Open discussion |
| 5 | Improvement Measures Development (technical, process, personnel) | 20 minutes | O&M project manager |
| 6 | Action Plan Assignment (responsible persons, deadlines) | 10 minutes | O&M project manager |
| 7 | Meeting Summary | 5 minutes | Chairperson |

### 5.11.2 Improvement Item Tracking Table

| Improvement Item ID | Improvement Item Description | Source Fault | Improvement Type | Responsible Person | Planned Completion Date | Actual Completion Date | Status | Effect Verification |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|

| IMP-002 | Increase UPS battery inspection frequency | 2026-06-05 power anomaly | Preventive measure | Hardware engineer | 2026-06-10 | Completed | Verified |

### 5.11.3 Effect Verification Methods

**Quantitative Verification:**
- Compare fault occurrence rates before and after improvement (monthly/quarterly year-over-year comparison);
- Compare Mean Time To Recovery (MTTR) before and after improvement;
- Compare system availability before and after improvement.

**Qualitative Verification:**
- Organize technical experts to review the effectiveness of improvement measures;
- Collect O&M team feedback on improvement measures;
- Evaluate the implementation difficulty and operability of improvement measures.

**Verification Cycle:**
- First verification 30 days after improvement measure implementation;
- Second verification 90 days after improvement measure implementation;
- Comprehensive evaluation quarterly.

## 5.12 Fault Prevention Strategy

### 5.12.1 Trend Analysis Methods

**Monthly Trend Analysis:**
- Compile monthly fault totals, fault counts by level, fault counts by system;
- Calculate month-over-month and year-over-year fault growth rates;
- Identify high-fault periods (by hour, by day of week, by month);
- Analyze fault type distribution (hardware/software/network/security/infrastructure).

**Quarterly Trend Analysis:**
- Analyze quarterly fault trends and identify seasonal patterns;
- Evaluate the effectiveness of preventive measures;
- Identify recurring faults and high-frequency faults;
- Develop next quarter's preventive maintenance priorities.

**Annual Trend Analysis:**
- Analyze annual fault trends and evaluate system reliability changes;
- Evaluate equipment aging trends and develop equipment replacement plans;
- Evaluate personnel skill improvement effectiveness;
- Develop next year's fault prevention strategy.

### 5.12.2 Weakness Identification

**Identification Methods:**
- Fault Frequency Analysis: Compile fault frequency for each system/equipment to identify high-frequency fault points;
- Fault Impact Analysis: Evaluate the impact of each system/equipment fault on business operations;
- Risk Assessment Matrix: Plot fault probability and impact degree on a risk matrix to identify high-risk areas;
- Lifespan Assessment: Based on equipment service life and operating status, evaluate equipment aging risks.

**Risk Assessment Matrix:**

| Fault Probability ＼ Impact Level | Low Impact | Medium Impact | High Impact | Severe Impact |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Very High (≥10 times/month) | Medium Risk | High Risk | Very High Risk | Very High Risk |
| High (5-10 times/month) | Low Risk | Medium Risk | High Risk | Very High Risk |
| Medium (2-5 times/month) | Low Risk | Medium Risk | Medium Risk | High Risk |
| Low (<2 times/month) | Low Risk | Low Risk | Medium Risk | Medium Risk |

### 5.12.3 Preventive Measures Tracking Table

| Prevention ID | Preventive Measure Description | Target Issue | Responsible Person | Planned Implementation Date | Actual Implementation Date | Implementation Status | Effect Evaluation |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|

| PREV-002 | Replace aging UPS battery packs | Insufficient UPS power supply duration | Hardware engineer | 2026-06-20 | In progress | Pending evaluation |
| PREV-003 | Upgrade core switch firmware | Intermittent switch packet loss | Network engineer | 2026-06-10 | Completed | Effective |

## 5.15 SLA Indicator Refinement

### 5.15.1 Availability Indicators

**System Availability Calculation Formula:**
```
System Availability = (Total Time - Fault Time) ÷ Total Time × 100%
```

**System Availability Targets:**

| System Name | Monthly Availability Target | Annual Availability Target | Allowed Monthly Downtime |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Core Business Systems | 99.99% | 99.95% | ≤4.32 minutes |
| Important Business Systems | 99.95% | 99.9% | ≤21.6 minutes |
| General Business Systems | 99.9% | 99.5% | ≤43.2 minutes |
| Infrastructure | 99.99% | 99.95% | ≤4.32 minutes |

### 5.15.2 MTTR (Mean Time To Recovery)

**MTTR Calculation Formula:**
```
MTTR = Total Recovery Time ÷ Number of Faults
```

**MTTR Target Values:**

| Fault Level | MTTR Target | MTTR Upper Limit | Assessment Period |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| P1 Level | ≤30 minutes | ≤60 minutes | Monthly |
| P2 Level | ≤1 hour | ≤2 hours | Monthly |
| P3 Level | ≤2 hours | ≤4 hours | Monthly |
| P4 Level | ≤4 hours | ≤8 hours | Monthly |

### 5.15.3 MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures)

**MTBF Calculation Formula:**
```
MTBF = Total Operating Time ÷ Number of Faults
```

**MTBF Target Values:**

| System Type | MTBF Target | Assessment Period |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Servers | ≥720 hours (30 days) | Monthly |
| Network Equipment | ≥8,760 hours (365 days) | Annual |
| Security Equipment | ≥8,760 hours (365 days) | Annual |
| Terminal Equipment | ≥2,160 hours (90 days) | Quarterly |

### 5.15.4 Fault Rate Indicators

**Fault Rate Calculation Formula:**
```
Fault Rate = Number of Faults ÷ Total Operating Time × 100%
```

**Fault Rate Target Values:**

| Fault Type | Monthly Fault Rate Target | Assessment Period |
|:---|:---|:---|
| P1-Level Faults | ≤0.1 times/month | Monthly |
| P2-Level Faults | ≤1 time/month | Monthly |
| P3-Level Faults | ≤5 times/month | Monthly |
| P4-Level Faults | ≤10 times/month | Monthly |

### 5.16.3 Escalation Notification Process

**Automatic Escalation Notification:**
- When fault handling reaches the automatic escalation time limit, the system automatically sends escalation notifications to the next-level responsible person;
- Escalation notifications include fault details, measures taken, escalation reason, and resources requiring coordination;
- Escalation notifications are sent simultaneously via SMS + email + system notification.

**Manual Escalation Notification:**
- When handling personnel determine escalation is needed, they fill out an escalation request form;
- After the escalation request form is confirmed by the next-level responsible person, it officially takes effect;
- After escalation takes effect, the system automatically notifies all relevant parties.

## 5.17 Third-Party Fault Coordination Mechanism

### 5.17.1 Vendor Contact List

| No. | Vendor Name | Responsible Project | Contact Person | Phone Number | Service Level | Response Time |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 1 | XX Technology Company | Server Equipment | Engineer Zhang | 138XXXX1001 | 7×24 hours | ≤2 hours |
| 2 | XX Network Company | Network Equipment | Engineer Li | 138XXXX1002 | 7×24 hours | ≤2 hours |
| 3 | XX Software Company | Application Software | Engineer Wang | 138XXXX1003 | 5×8 hours | ≤4 hours |
| 4 | XX Operator | Network Lines | Manager Zhao | 138XXXX1004 | 7×24 hours | ≤1 hour |
| 5 | XX Security Company | Security Equipment | Engineer Sun | 138XXXX1005 | 5×8 hours | ≤8 hours |
| 6 | XX Power Company | Power Supply Facilities | Engineer Zhou | 138XXXX1006 | 7×24 hours | ≤30 minutes |

### 5.17.2 Joint Handling Process

**Third-Party Fault Handling Process:**
1. O&M team confirms the fault involves third-party equipment or services;
2. O&M project manager contacts the corresponding vendor liaison person, reporting fault details;
3. Vendor confirms whether the fault falls within their responsibility scope;
4. If it falls within the vendor's responsibility, the vendor responds to the fault according to their SLA;
5. O&M team tracks third-party handling progress throughout;
6. After fault recovery, both parties confirm the handling result;
7. O&M team prepares a third-party fault handling record.

**Joint Handling Meetings:**
- For complex third-party faults, the O&M project manager convenes a joint handling meeting;
- Meeting participants: O&M team, vendor technical team, Procuring Entity representative;
- Meeting content: Fault cause analysis, responsibility delineation, handling plan, preventive measures;
- Meeting minutes are prepared by the O&M team and signed by all parties for confirmation.

### 5.17.3 Responsibility Delineation

**Responsibility Delineation Principles:**
- During equipment warranty period: Equipment hardware faults are the responsibility of the equipment vendor;
- During software license period: Software defects are the responsibility of the software vendor;
- During service contract period: Faults within the service scope are the responsibility of the service provider;
- Human operational errors: The responsibility of the operating party;
- Force majeure: Shared through negotiation among all parties.

**Responsibility Delineation Process:**
1. After a fault occurs, the O&M team makes a preliminary determination of the responsible party;
2. If multiple parties are involved, the O&M project manager organizes a responsibility delineation meeting;
3. Each party provides evidence (logs, monitoring data, operational records, etc.);
4. Based on evidence and contract terms, determine each party's responsibility ratio;
5. Prepare a responsibility delineation report, signed by all parties for confirmation.

## 5.18 Fault Handling Drill Plan

### 5.18.1 Tabletop Drill Plan

**Drill Purpose:** Verify the completeness and operability of emergency response plans, enhance team collaboration capabilities.

**Drill Frequency:** Once per quarter

**Drill Process:**

| Phase | Content | Duration | Responsible Person |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Preparation | Determine drill scenario, prepare drill script, notify participants | 3 days | O&M project manager |
| Launch | Announce drill start, distribute drill script | 10 minutes | Drill facilitator |
| Walkthrough | Walk through fault handling process step by step per script | 60-90 minutes | All participants |
| Discussion | Participants discuss issues and improvement points from the drill | 30 minutes | All participants |
| Summary | Prepare drill summary report | 1 day | O&M project manager |

**Tabletop Drill Scenario Examples:**
- Scenario 1: Core database server downtime, requiring switch to backup server;
- Scenario 2: Core network switch failure, requiring activation of backup link;
- Scenario 3: Ransomware attack, requiring isolation of infected area and data recovery;
- Scenario 4: Data center power outage, requiring backup generator activation.

### 5.18.2 Live Drill Plan

**Drill Purpose:** Verify emergency response capabilities in an actual environment and validate the feasibility of technical solutions.

**Drill Frequency:** Once every six months

**Drill Process:**

| Phase | Content | Duration | Responsible Person |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Planning | Determine drill plan, risk assessment, develop safety plan | 2 weeks | O&M project manager |
| Preparation | Prepare drill environment, backup data, notify relevant parties | 1 week | O&M team |
| Implementation | Execute drill operations in actual environment | 2-4 hours | All participants |
| Recovery | Restore drill environment to normal state | 1 hour | O&M team |
| Evaluation | Prepare drill evaluation report, propose improvement suggestions | 3 days | O&M project manager |

**Live Drill Scenario Examples:**
- Scenario 1: Simulate core server failure, execute system switching operations;
- Scenario 2: Simulate network interruption, execute backup link switching operations;
- Scenario 3: Simulate data corruption, execute data recovery operations;
- Scenario 4: Simulate power supply failure, execute backup power switching operations.

### 5.18.3 Drill Evaluation Standards

**Evaluation Dimensions:**

| Evaluation Dimension | Evaluation Indicator | Weight | Scoring Criteria |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Response Speed | Time from fault discovery to response initiation | 20% | Full score for ≤5 min, deduct 5 points per additional minute |
| Handling Efficiency | Time from response initiation to business recovery | 25% | Full score for within SLA limit, deduct 5 points per 10% excess |
| Collaboration Capability | Smoothness of team coordination and information transmission | 20% | Full score for no delays, deduct 5 points per delay |
| Plan Effectiveness | Scientific rigor and operability of handling plan | 20% | Full score for reasonable plan, deduct 5 points per unreasonable element |
| Documentation Completeness | Completeness and accuracy of drill records | 15% | Full score for complete records, deduct 3 points per omission |

**Evaluation Grades:**
- Excellent (≥90 points): Drill effect is good, can be directly applied to actual situations;
- Good (80-89 points): Drill effect is relatively good, minor improvements needed;
- Pass (70-79 points): Drill effect is average, key improvements needed;
- Fail (<70 points): Drill effect is poor, drill needs to be reorganized.

## 5.21 Fault Handling Quality Evaluation

### 5.21.1 Handling Timeliness Evaluation

**Evaluation Indicators:**

| Indicator Name | Calculation Formula | Target Value | Weight |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Response Timeliness Rate | Work orders responded within specified time ÷ Total work orders × 100% | ≥98% | 25% |
| Arrival Timeliness Rate | Work orders arrived within specified time ÷ Total work orders × 100% | ≥95% | 25% |
| Recovery Timeliness Rate | Work orders recovered within specified time ÷ Total work orders × 100% | ≥97% | 30% |
| First-Visit Fix Rate | Work orders fixed on first visit ÷ Total on-site work orders × 100% | ≥85% | 20% |

### 5.21.2 Customer Satisfaction Evaluation

**Satisfaction Survey Dimensions:**

| Survey Dimension | Survey Question Example | Scoring Standard |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Response Speed | Are you satisfied with the fault response speed? | 1-5 points |
| Service Attitude | Are you satisfied with the engineer's service attitude? | 1-5 points |
| Professional Level | Are you satisfied with the engineer's professional capability? | 1-5 points |
| Handling Effect | Was the fault completely resolved? | 1-5 points |
| Communication Quality | Are you satisfied with the communication during handling? | 1-5 points |
| Overall Evaluation | What is your overall satisfaction with this service? | 1-5 points |

**Satisfaction Targets:**
- Monthly average satisfaction ≥4.0 points (out of 5);
- Proportion of satisfaction ≥4 points ≥80%;
- Proportion of satisfaction ≤2 points ≤5%.

### 5.21.3 Recurrence Rate Evaluation

**Recurrence Rate Calculation Formula:**
```
Fault Recurrence Rate = Number of times the same fault recurs within 30 days ÷ Total occurrences of that fault × 100%
```

**Recurrence Rate Targets:**
- P1-level fault recurrence rate: ≤1% (target 0%)
- P2-level fault recurrence rate: ≤3%
- P3-level fault recurrence rate: ≤5%
- P4-level fault recurrence rate: ≤10%

**Handling Measures for Excessive Recurrence Rates:**
- When recurrence rate exceeds the threshold, special analysis must be organized within 48 hours;
- Use root cause analysis methods (5-Why / Fishbone Diagram / FTA) for in-depth analysis;
- Develop targeted preventive measures to reduce fault recurrence rates;
- Track the implementation and effectiveness of improvement measures.

## 5.23 Fault Handling Automation Plan

### 5.23.1 Automatic Diagnosis Rules

**Automatic Diagnosis Rules Table:**

| Rule ID | Rule Name | Trigger Condition | Diagnosis Logic | Automatic Action |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| AD-001 | High CPU Usage Alert | CPU usage >90% for 5 minutes | Check process list, identify high-CPU processes | Send alert + record log |
| AD-002 | High Memory Usage Alert | Memory usage >90% for 5 minutes | Check memory allocation, identify memory leaks | Send alert + record log |
| AD-003 | Low Disk Space Alert | Disk usage >85% | Check large files and temporary files | Send alert + clean temporary files |
| AD-004 | Network Connectivity Alert | Ping latency >100ms or packet loss >1% | Check network device status and link quality | Send alert + record log |
| AD-005 | Service Process Anomaly Alert | Critical service process does not exist | Check service process status | Send alert + attempt service restart |
| AD-006 | Database Connection Anomaly Alert | Database connections > threshold | Check slow queries and lock waits | Send alert + record log |

### 5.23.2 Automatic Recovery Scripts

**Automatic Recovery Scripts List:**

| Script ID | Script Name | Applicable Scenario | Recovery Logic | Execution Condition |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| AR-001 | Service Auto-Restart | Critical service process anomaly | Detect service process status, auto-restart when anomalous | Service process does not exist and restart count <3 |
| AR-002 | Disk Space Auto-Cleanup | Disk usage >90% | Clean temporary files, log files, recycle bin | Disk usage >90% |
| AR-003 | Network Link Auto-Switch | Primary network link interruption | Detect link status, auto-switch to backup link | Primary link Ping fails for 30 seconds |
| AR-004 | Database Connection Auto-Release | Database connections exceed limit | Identify long-idle connections and release | Connections exceed 80% of threshold |
| AR-005 | Load Balancing Auto-Adjustment | Uneven server load | Adjust traffic distribution based on load conditions | Load difference exceeds 30% |

### 5.23.3 Self-Healing Mechanism

**Self-Healing Mechanism Design:**

| Self-Healing Level | Applicable Scenario | Self-Healing Action | Manual Intervention Condition |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| L1 - Fully Automatic | Simple, standardized faults | Fully automatic recovery, no manual intervention required | Notify manual handling when auto-recovery fails |
| L2 - Semi-Automatic | Faults requiring confirmation | Auto-execute recovery plan, manual confirmation required before activation | Manual confirmation required before recovery |
| L3 - Assisted | Complex faults | Auto-collect information, generate plan, manual execution | Fully manual-led |

**Self-Healing Mechanism Safety Assurance:**
- All automatic recovery scripts must undergo rigorous testing before deployment;
- All automatic recovery operations are fully logged for post-incident auditing;
- Recovery attempt limits are set to prevent infinite recovery loops;
- When automatic recovery fails, automatically escalate to manual handling;
- Automatic recovery rules are periodically reviewed and updated.

## 5.24 Cross-Department Coordination Mechanism

### 5.24.1 Responsibility Delineation

**Departmental Responsibilities in Fault Handling:**

| Department | Responsibility Scope | Main Tasks | Collaboration Method |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| O&M Team | Primary fault handling force | Fault diagnosis, repair, recovery | Lead handling |
| Development Team | Application system support | Software defect repair, performance optimization | Technical support |
| Information Security Department | Security incident handling | Security incident investigation, handling | Security support |
| Procuring Entity O&M Management | Supervision and coordination | Fault confirmation, acceptance, feedback | Supervision and coordination |
| Procuring Entity Business Departments | Business impact assessment | Business alternative plan execution | Business cooperation |
| Equipment Vendors | Hardware technical support | Hardware fault diagnosis and repair | External support |
| Operators | Line technical support | Line fault investigation and repair | External support |

### 5.24.2 Collaboration Process

**Cross-Department Fault Handling Process:**
1. O&M team confirms the fault requires cross-department collaboration;
2. O&M project manager contacts relevant department heads;
3. Convene a cross-department coordination meeting to clarify each party's responsibilities;
4. Each party carries out handling work according to their assignment;
5. O&M team uniformly coordinates the actions of all parties;
6. After fault recovery, all parties confirm the handling result;
7. O&M team prepares a cross-department collaboration summary report.

### 5.24.3 Information Sharing Mechanism

**Information Sharing Platform:**
- O&M Management System: Fault work orders, handling progress, handling results;
- WeCom/DingTalk: Real-time communication, file sharing, video conferencing;
- Shared Document Library: Technical documentation, operational manuals, emergency plans;
- Email System: Formal notifications, report distribution, meeting minutes.

**Information Sharing Standards:**
- P1-level fault information must be notified to all relevant departments within 5 minutes;
- P2-level fault information must be notified to relevant departments within 15 minutes;
- Fault handling progress must be updated every 30 minutes;
- Formal notification must be sent to all relevant departments within 24 hours after fault recovery.

## 5.25 Fault Handling Performance Evaluation

### 5.25.1 Evaluation Indicator System

| Evaluation Dimension | Evaluation Indicator | Target Value | Weight | Data Source |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Response Efficiency | Average Response Time | ≤SLA limit | 20% | O&M Management System |
| Handling Quality | First-Visit Fix Rate | ≥85% | 20% | O&M Management System |
| Recovery Efficiency | Average Recovery Time | ≤SLA limit | 20% | O&M Management System |
| Customer Satisfaction | Satisfaction Score | ≥4.0 points | 15% | Satisfaction Survey |
| Collaboration Capability | Cross-Department Collaboration Evaluation | ≥80 points | 10% | Collaborator Evaluation |
| Documentation Quality | Work Order Report Completeness | 100% | 10% | Quality Inspection Records |
| Training Participation | Training Completion Rate | 100% | 5% | Training Records |

### 5.25.2 Evaluation Cycle and Methods

**Monthly Evaluation:**
- Complete previous month's evaluation by the 5th of each month;
- Evaluation data automatically collected by the O&M management system;
- Evaluation results linked to monthly performance bonus.

**Quarterly Evaluation:**
- Comprehensive evaluation at the end of each quarter;
- Includes monthly evaluation average (60%) + quarterly comprehensive evaluation (40%);
- Evaluation results linked to quarterly performance bonus and promotion.

**Annual Evaluation:**
- Annual evaluation in December each year;
- Includes quarterly evaluation average (60%) + annual comprehensive evaluation (40%);
- Evaluation results linked to annual bonus, promotion, and position transfer.

### 5.25.3 Reward and Penalty Measures

**Reward Measures:**
- Monthly evaluation excellent (≥90 points): Performance bonus increase of 10%;
- Quarterly evaluation excellent (≥90 points): Performance bonus increase of 15%, priority promotion;
- Annual evaluation excellent (≥90 points): Year-end bonus increase of 20%, priority promotion;
- Major contribution (successful handling of P1-level fault): Special reward.

**Penalty Measures:**
- Monthly evaluation fail (<70 points): Performance bonus decrease of 10%, attend remedial training;
- Quarterly evaluation fail (<70 points): Performance bonus decrease of 20%, demotion;
- Annual evaluation fail (<70 points): Year-end bonus canceled, position transfer or termination;
- Major fault (fault escalation caused by human factors): Special penalty.

- Major modifications (V2.0 and above) must be approved by the O&M project manager.

- Paper documents are stored in dedicated filing cabinets;
- Important documents must have off-site backups;
- Document completeness and readability are periodically checked.

## 5.28 Continuous Improvement Mechanism

### 5.28.1 PDCA Continuous Improvement Cycle

**Plan:**
- Develop fault handling improvement plan at the beginning of each quarter;
- Specify improvement objectives, measures, responsible persons, and deadlines;
- Improvement plans must be approved by the O&M project manager.

**Do:**
- Execute improvement measures according to the improvement plan;
- Record the implementation status of improvement measures;
- Provide timely feedback and adjustment when issues are encountered.

**Check:**
- Evaluate the effectiveness of improvement measures at the end of each quarter;
- Compare key indicator changes before and after improvement;
- Identify shortcomings in improvement measures and new improvement opportunities.

**Act:**
- Codify effective improvement measures into standard procedures;
- Adjust improvement measures that did not meet expectations;
- Incorporate new improvement opportunities into the next improvement cycle.

### 5.28.2 Improvement Suggestion Collection Channels

| Collection Channel | Collection Frequency | Collection Method | Processing Flow |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Fault Retrospective Meetings | After each P1/P2 level fault | Meeting discussion | Record → Review → Implement → Verify |
| Customer Feedback | Continuous | Satisfaction survey | Compile → Analyze → Improve → Feedback |
| O&M Team Suggestions | Monthly | Team meeting | Collect → Review → Implement → Track |
| Management Review | Quarterly | Management review meeting | Deliberate → Decide → Deploy → Track |
| External Audit | Annual | Third-party audit | Receive → Rectify → Verify → Report |

### 5.28.3 Improvement Effect Evaluation Methods

**Quantitative Evaluation:**
- Fault rate change trends (monthly/quarterly/annual comparison);
- MTTR change trends;
- System availability change trends;
- Customer satisfaction change trends.

**Qualitative Evaluation:**
- O&M team satisfaction with improvement measures;
- Management evaluation of improvement effectiveness;
- Collaborator evaluation of collaboration efficiency.

**Evaluation Cycle:**
- Short-term evaluation (30 days after improvement measure implementation);
- Medium-term evaluation (90 days after improvement measure implementation);
- Long-term evaluation (365 days after improvement measure implementation).

# Chapter 6 Service Assurance


## 6.1 Operations and Maintenance Personnel Organization

### 6.1.1 Organizational Structure

The operations and maintenance (O&M) service for this project adopts a four-tier organizational structure system of "Company Management — Project Management — On-site Service — Remote Support," forming a unified, clearly-divided, collaborative, and efficient O&M management team.

**Company Management**: Led by the company's executive leader, responsible for major project decisions, resource allocation, and client relationship maintenance, bearing overall responsibility for the project's service quality.

**Project Management**: Composed of the Project Director and Project Manager, responsible for daily project operations management, service quality monitoring, client communication and coordination, and team management.

**On-site Service**: Composed of the On-site Technical Lead and On-site O&M Engineers, responsible for the purchaser's on-site daily O&M work, including equipment inspection, fault handling, system maintenance, and technical support.

**Remote Support**: Composed of remote technical support engineers, providing backend technical support for the on-site team, including difficult problem resolution, performance optimization, security monitoring, and technical consultation.

This project has established 18 O&M management positions. The responsibilities, authority, reporting relationships, and qualification requirements for each position are clearly defined as follows:

3. Responsible for communication with the purchaser's senior leadership, timely understanding of the purchaser's needs and expectations

6. Organize important project meetings and technical reviews
7. Responsible for the construction and management of the project O&M team

10. Review project service reports and bear overall responsibility for project service quality
11. Promote project management innovation and the application of best practices

**Position Authority**:

### 6.1.4 On-site Personnel AB Post Mechanism

To ensure the continuity and stability of on-site services, this project implements a strict AB post (backup post) mechanism. Specific requirements are as follows:

#### (I) AB Post Configuration Plan

| Primary Post (A Post) | Backup Post (B Post) | Remarks |
|:---|:---|:---|
| On-site Technical Lead | Remote Technical Support Engineer (concurrent) | When the Technical Lead is on business trip or leave, the designated remote engineer temporarily assumes the On-site Technical Lead responsibilities |
| On-site O&M Engineer A | On-site O&M Engineer B | Mutual backup, ensuring at least 1 O&M engineer is on duty at all times |
| On-site O&M Engineer B | On-site O&M Engineer A | Mutual backup |
| Project Manager | Project Director (concurrent) | When the Project Manager is absent, the Project Director temporarily assumes the Project Manager responsibilities |

#### (II) AB Post Handover Process

```
┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐
│A Post    │───▶│ Advance  │───▶│B Post    │───▶│ Work     │
│Leave     │    │ Notice   │    │Confirms  │    │ Handover │
│(3 days   │    │ to PM    │    │Task      │    │ Item-by- │
│ in adv.) │    │          │    │Acceptance│    │ Item     │
└──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘
                                                       │
                                                       ▼
┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐
│A Post    │◀───│ Handover │◀───│ Work     │◀───│B Post    │
│Returns & │    │ Sign-back│    │ Summary  │    │ Assumes  │
│Confirms  │    │ Both     │    │ Records  │    │ Duties & │
│Receipt   │    │ Sign     │    │ Archived │    │ Full Log │
└──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘
```

#### (III) AB Post Management Requirements

1. **Advance Notice System**: A-post personnel unable to report for duty must submit a written notice to the Project Manager 3 working days in advance, stating the reason, departure time, and expected return time.
2. **Work Handover Checklist**: Before A-post departure, a handover must be conducted with B-post item by item, completing the "AB Post Work Handover Record Form." Content includes but is not limited to: ongoing work tasks, pending items, key focus areas, incomplete items, important contacts, etc.
3. **Seamless Transition**: B-post personnel must fully assume A-post responsibilities during the A-post absence period, ensuring service quality does not decline and work is not interrupted.
4. **Emergency Replacement**: If A-post personnel cannot report for duty due to unforeseen circumstances and cannot provide advance notice, the Project Manager shall designate B-post personnel for emergency replacement, with handover procedures to be completed afterward.
5. **Equivalent Capability**: B-post personnel must possess technical capabilities and service levels comparable to A-post. We will regularly organize cross-training for AB post personnel to ensure equivalent capabilities.

### 6.1.5 Personnel Attendance Management System

#### (I) Attendance Methods

1. **On-site Personnel**: Adopt a dual attendance method of "facial recognition check-in + electronic sign-in," with check-in once each at the beginning and end of the workday.
2. **Remote Personnel**: Adopt an "online sign-in + work record" method, signing in daily in the work group and recording the day's work content.
3. **Project Director and Project Manager**: Adopt an "on-site as needed + remote work" method, with on-site attendance following on-site personnel standards on days they report to the office.

#### (II) Attendance Hours

| Type | Start Time | End Time | Lunch Break |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Workdays | 08:00 | 18:00 | 12:00-14:00 |
| On-call Days | 09:00 | 17:00 | — |
| Emergency Periods | 24/7 response | — | — |

#### (III) Leave System

| Leave Type | Approval Authority | Advance Notice Period | Remarks |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Personal Leave | Project Manager approval | 1 day in advance | B-post replacement must be arranged |
| Sick Leave | Project Manager approval | Same day | Medical certificate required |
| Annual Leave | Project Director approval | 7 days in advance | Work must be arranged in advance |
| Compensatory Leave | Project Manager approval | 1 day in advance | Must be used within the same month |
| Marriage/Bereavement Leave | Project Director approval | 3 days in advance | Per national regulations |

#### (IV) Attendance Rewards and Penalties

1. **Full Attendance Bonus**: Monthly full attendance (no tardiness, early departure, absenteeism, or leave) receives a full attendance bonus of 500 CNY per person.
2. **Tardiness/Early Departure**: Tardiness or early departure within 15 minutes incurs a deduction of 50 CNY per occurrence; exceeding 15 minutes but less than 1 hour incurs a deduction of 100 CNY per occurrence; exceeding 1 hour is treated as half-day absenteeism.
3. **Absenteeism**: Half-day absenteeism incurs a deduction of 200 CNY, full-day absenteeism incurs a deduction of 500 CNY. Consecutive absenteeism for 3 or more days is considered a serious violation of management rules and may result in replacement.
4. **Overtime Compensation**: Overtime arranged due to work needs shall be compensated at national standard rates or with compensatory time off.

## 6.2 Quality Assurance Measures

### 6.2.1 Service Availability Assurance

#### (I) Network Availability Assurance (Target: 99.99%)

To ensure network availability reaches 99.99% (annual downtime not exceeding 52.6 minutes), we adopt the following assurance measures:

1. **Redundancy Design**: Core network equipment uses dual hot-standby configuration, critical links use dual-path redundancy, and automatic failover occurs upon any equipment or link failure.
2. **Real-time Monitoring**: Deploy network monitoring systems (Zabbix/Prometheus) for 7×24-hour real-time monitoring of network equipment and link status, with fault detection time not exceeding 1 minute.
3. **Preventive Maintenance**: Conduct monthly network equipment health checks, including CPU/memory utilization, port status, link quality, etc., to identify and address potential issues in advance.
4. **Rapid Response**: Upon network equipment failure, initiate emergency response plan within 15 minutes, and restore network service within 30 minutes (via backup equipment or backup links).
5. **Bandwidth Management**: Implement bandwidth monitoring and traffic management to ensure bandwidth reservation for critical business operations and prevent service interruptions caused by bandwidth congestion.
6. **Link Redundancy**: Internet exit uses dual-carrier dual-link redundancy with automatic failover.

**Table 6-5 Network Availability Indicator Breakdown**

| Protection Target | Availability Target | Annual Allowed Downtime | Protection Measures |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Core Switches | 99.999% | ≤5.26 minutes | Dual hot-standby + Fast failover |
| Aggregation Switches | 99.99% | ≤52.6 minutes | Redundant links + Fast recovery |
| Exit Firewalls | 99.99% | ≤52.6 minutes | Dual hot-standby + Policy synchronization |
| Internet Links | 99.99% | ≤52.6 minutes | Dual-carrier redundancy |
| Wireless Network | 99.95% | ≤4.38 hours | AP redundant coverage + Auto-optimization |

#### (II) System Availability Assurance (Target: 99.95%)

To ensure system availability reaches 99.95% (annual downtime not exceeding 4.38 hours), we adopt the following assurance measures:

1. **Server High Availability**: Critical application servers use cluster deployment, with single-node failure not affecting business continuity.
2. **Database High Availability**: Databases use master-slave replication or cluster architecture to ensure high availability of database services.
3. **Storage High Availability**: Storage systems use RAID protection + data replication to ensure data security and availability.
4. **Automated Monitoring and Alerting**: Deploy a system monitoring platform for comprehensive monitoring of servers, databases, middleware, and application systems, with automatic anomaly alerting.
5. **Regular Backups**: Establish a comprehensive backup strategy with daily incremental backups and weekly full backups to ensure data recoverability.
6. **Rapid Recovery**: Upon system failure, complete fault identification within 30 minutes and restore system service within 2 hours (RTO ≤ 2 hours), with data recovery point objective (RPO) ≤ 1 hour.
